claims.text: The low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are governed by intrinsic dynamic recovery.
Fast dislocation cross-slip and annihilation limit dislocation-density buildup and forest hardening during deformation.
The applicable composition is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The starting material is a fully homogenized, coarse-grained, single-phase solid solution.
Temperature and strain rate will be varied during controlled cold compression or tension.
Coarse-grained and refined-grained samples will be compared to modulate dislocation accumulation.
Dynamic recovery is active under quasi-static loading at room temperature and moderately elevated temperatures in this alloy.
The relevant structural mediators are dislocation-network density and arrangement, together with low-angle subgrain boundaries formed through cross-slip-related processes.
The chemically disordered CoCrFeNiTi matrix has relatively low stacking-fault energy.
Relatively low stacking-fault energy facilitates easy cross-slip and dynamic recovery.
Dislocation rearrangement and annihilation prevent strong pileups and limit work hardening.
Limited work hardening produces lower hardness and strength while retaining good ductility.
Higher temperature will promote dynamic recovery, reduce strain hardening, and produce steady-state flow at lower dislocation density.
Coarser grains will favor dislocation mobility and dynamic recovery, leading to lower strain hardening and lower dislocation density.
Grain refinement or lower temperature will suppress recovery and increase strain hardening, hardness, and strength.

The proposed mechanism applies only to single-phase simple-solid-solution HEAs without secondary precipitates or intermetallic phases and at moderate strain rates and temperatures where recovery is kinetically active.
TEM measurements of dislocation density, subgrain-boundary fraction, and cross-slip-related structures can test the proposed recovery mechanism.

The hypothesis is falsified if conditions intended to alter recovery produce no significant differences in work hardening or dislocation/subgrain structures, or if dislocation density accumulates similarly in all conditions.
The role of Ti-induced local lattice distortion and the quantitative effect of stacking-fault-energy variations remain uncertain.
